e-6629.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
e-6629.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
x^2 y'' + xy' + 4y = 0,\quad x > 0.
$$
e-6629.worked_solution:
This is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume the solutions take the form $y=x^\lambda.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
y' = \lambda x^{\lambda -1}, \qquad y'' = \lambda(\lambda-1)x^{\lambda-2}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+4{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+4{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +4] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)=c_1 \cos( 2 \ln{x} )  + c_2\sin( 2 \ln{x} ).
$$

decision.explanation: Substituting y=x^λ gives λ(λ−1)+λ+16=λ²+16=0, so λ=±4i. Thus the general solution is c₁cos(4ln x)+c₂sin(4ln x), option d. Option b describes the same solution family because 4ln(2x)=4ln x+4ln 2 is a constant phase shift.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+16y=0,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+16{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+16{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +16] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, we note

$$

$$

$$

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

a
y(x)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡4x)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡4x)

y(x)=c1cos⁡(4ln⁡2x)+c2sin⁡(4ln⁡2x)

EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2+x⋅λxλ−1+16xλ=0λ(λ−1)xλ+λxλ+16xλ=0xλ[λ(λ−1)+λ+16]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)+λ+16=0λ2+16=0λ2=−16.

Hence, the roots are λ=±4i.

Now, we note

x4i=eln⁡x4i=e4iln⁡x=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+isin⁡(4ln⁡x),x−4i=eln⁡x−4i=e−4iln⁡x=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−isin⁡(4ln⁡x).

Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=Ax4i+Bx−4iy(x)=A(cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+isin⁡(4ln⁡x))+B(cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−isin⁡(4ln⁡x))y(x)=(A+B)cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+i(A−B)sin⁡(4ln⁡x).

Finally, we can rewrite y(x) as y(x)=c1cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(4ln⁡x),

where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+16y=0,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+16{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+16{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +16] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, we note

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{\text{4i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{\text{4i}}}={e}^{\text{4i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x), \\ {x}^{-\text{4i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-\text{4i}}}={e}^{-\text{4i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{\text{4i}}+B{x}^{-\text{4i}} \\ y(x) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ y(x) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+y=0,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +1] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm \text{i}.$

Now, we note

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x), \\ {x}^{-\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{\text{i}}+B{x}^{-\text{i}} \\ y(x) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ y(x) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x),

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)+λ+1=0λ2+1=0λ2=−1.

Hence, the roots are λ=±i.

Now, we note

xi=eln⁡xi=eiln⁡x=cos⁡(ln⁡x)+isin⁡(ln⁡x),x−i=eln⁡x−i=e−iln⁡x=cos⁡(ln⁡x)−isin⁡(ln⁡x).

content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+y=0,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +1] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm \text{i}.$

Now, we note

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x), \\ {x}^{-\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{\text{i}}+B{x}^{-\text{i}} \\ y(x) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ y(x) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+7y=0,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +7] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +7 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+7 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{7}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{\sqrt{7}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{\sqrt{7}\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\ {t}^{-\sqrt{7}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{-\sqrt{7}\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$

content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+7y=0,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +7] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +7 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+7 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{7}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{\sqrt{7}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{\sqrt{7}\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\ {t}^{-\sqrt{7}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{-\sqrt{7}\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{\sqrt{7}\text{i}}+B{t}^{-\sqrt{7}\text{i}} \\ y(t) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ y(t) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

decision.explanation: Dividing by 3 gives t²y″+ty′+6y=0. Substituting y=t^λ yields λ²+6=0, so λ=±i√6. Thus the general solution is c₁cos(√6 ln t)+c₂sin(√6 ln t), option d.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
3{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+3t{y}^{′}+18y=0,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+3t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+18{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 3\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+3\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+18{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[3\lambda (\lambda -1)+3\lambda +18] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}3\lambda (\lambda -1)+3\lambda +18 & =0 \\ 3{\lambda }^{2}+18 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{6}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{\sqrt{6}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{\sqrt{6}\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\ {t}^{-\sqrt{6}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{-\sqrt{6}\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{\sqrt{6}\text{i}}+B{t}^{-\sqrt{6}\text{i}} \\ y(t) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ y(t) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
3{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+3t{y}^{′}+18y=0,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+3t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+18{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 3\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+3\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+18{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[3\lambda (\lambda -1)+3\lambda +18] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}3\lambda (\lambda -1)+3\lambda +18 & =0 \\ 3{\lambda }^{2}+18 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{6}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{\sqrt{6}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{\sqrt{6}\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\ {t}^{-\sqrt{6}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{-\sqrt{6}\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{\sqrt{6}\text{i}}+B{t}^{-\sqrt{6}\text{i}} \\ y(t) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ y(t) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+9y=0,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+9{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+9{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +9] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 3\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{3\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{3\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}3\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t), \\ {t}^{-3\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{-3\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}3\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{3\text{i}}+B{t}^{-3\text{i}} \\ y(t) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ y(t) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)+λ+9=0λ2+9=0λ2=−9.

Hence, the roots are λ=±3i.

Now, we note that

t3i=eln⁡t3i=ei3ln⁡t=cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+isin⁡(3ln⁡t),t−3i=eln⁡t−3i=e−i3ln⁡t=cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−isin⁡(3ln⁡t).

content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+9y=0,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+9{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+9{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +9] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 3\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{3\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{3\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}3\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t), \\ {t}^{-3\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{-3\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}3\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{3\text{i}}+B{t}^{-3\text{i}} \\ y(t) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ y(t) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$
